utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel, good morning everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, April Carter, and Inger de Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Before we go to you, Mr. Lukic, I'm on channel 4 but I'm hearing a language that is not English, and I don't know what it is I'm hearing. I think I'm hearing B/C/S. Does any other person have the same problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't have my headset on, Your Honour, but I'm told by Ms. Carter that she had a B/C/S and English overlay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't have English at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard you direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the stenographer heard you and could type you, that's fine. Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Just to place it on the record, the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today in the absence of Judge Picard. Good morning, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Petrovic, just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall continue where we left to off two days ago. There's a document that I would like to finish off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce D464 MFI, which is the excerpt from your financial file about the amounts received by yourself. As for the English, we can stick to the page that we have on the screen right now and can the box with number 1 be zoomed in for the witness, where it says "payments as per rank." This is exactly what has been translated into English actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the day before yesterday we looked at the bottom part and the data in the bottom part. I would like to see what data is entered in the box where it says Payment By Rank, and could you please provide a comment on the last entry. What does it refer to in this box? What promotion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be zoomed in a bit further for the witness on the screen. The left upper portion so I can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, Your Honours, in the column where it says Payment By Rank, this contains data on promotions pursuant to the orders on promotions, and the last or the fourth box means that there was an order pursuant to which I was promoted into captain 1st class on the 7th of January, 1993. It was an interim promotion and the order was issued by the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the one and the same order on promotion that we saw two days ago? Was the data from that order transferred into this box?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the data that was transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need this document. I will move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like you to tell us in just a few words, Mr. Petrovic, what did your administration deal with, what were its main tasks and duties, and within that framework what was your duty in that administration?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration where I was affiliated with was the administration for planning, development, and financing. Its task was to plan the required monetary resources for the Army of Republika Srpska. It also had to organise the execution of any such financial plan. It had to control, or rather, the internal control of the execution of the plan, it had to undertake analysis, reporting envisaged by the regulations. Its task was also to deal with regulations and the issues of bookkeeping and accountancy of property, moveable property of the army. It also dealt with the payment of salaries and a number of other activities that arose from the area of financing of the Army of Republika Srpska. Its tasks stemmed in practical terms from the nature of its organisation. Last time I told you what departments it had comprised, or rather, which departments made up the administration. Do you want me to repeat all these departments?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to. What were your tasks within your department, very specifically?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had been appointed as a member of one department, the department for plan and analysis, my task was to collect the information on the requirements of the corps, to analyse them, to summarise them, to prepare appropriate documents and enactments that would be signed by the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I then forwarded those documents to whoever they had to be forwarded to. I was involved in the execution of the financing plans. In 1992 there was a sub-account --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just stop here.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on, I have some other questions for you in order to cover this topic thoroughly. Before this Trial Chamber we already heard testimony about the budgetary part of the financing of the Army of Republika Srpska. In technical terms, how were budgetary allocations transferred to the end users? How was it done in different years?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 one and only possible modality of the execution of the budget was found. Those finances were approved by the Ministry of Defence to the Army of Republika Srpska. Because of the whirlwind of the war, sub-accounts were opened. There was the sub-account of the Main Staff and the sub-accounts of the corps. In keeping with the requirements which we received for the approval of financing and we forwarded to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, the funds were paid into the account of the Main Staff. In co-operation with the logistics sector of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, we analysed the requirements and needs of each of the corps and funds were transferred on to the sub-accounts of those corps and were segregated by different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who made those decisions for the funds to be distributed per different users?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made by the commander of the Main Staff, based on proposals and documents that had been prepared by the administration for planning. There was already co-operation in that area with the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I.e., for the rear sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any changes to that technology of the distribution of funds? What happened? Who was it who decided on any possible changes?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were different changes that took place, depending on the war circumstances. Better ways were sought and found to execute the budget. In late 1992 a decision was made on the setting up of the military accountancy centre based in Banja Luka. Its main task was to act on behalf of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska and to carry out payment transactions, to also carry out the internal control of all the documents based on which payments were executed. The accountancy centre also had all the records segregated by corps, purposes, or accounts of the then account classification that was applied in companies and offices. It also had to carry out a certain number of analyses, the same one that the administration had been engaged in while payments were executed via sub-accounts. Those analyses were then forwarded to the superior administration. That was the administration for planning, financing, and analysis of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to put that as a sub-question. You spoke about the military accountancy centre. Who was it subordinated to directly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military accountancy centre in Banja Luka was directly subordinated to the chief of the administration for planning, development, and financing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to move on to a different topic. In addition to the budgetary sources of financing, were there any other sources of financing for the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The budgetary funds represented only one of the sources of financing for the Army of Republika Srpska. There were also numerous donations, assistance, aid that came from citizens, associations, companies, both at the local level as well and especially so those contributions came from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In addition to the things that I've just mentioned, a significant source of financing, as it were, were donations of citizens' associations of Serbs who worked abroad. As for the local level of financing, companies that still operated or were still able to operate that employed people through work obligation, they also ensured quite a considerable amount of money for the army. Also, this was based on the decision of the local authorities or the government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You said that these donations came from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When you say that, which natural or legal persons do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, citizen associations, companies who would get organised and send aid and foodstuffs, clothing, or anything else which could be of use and which could meet the needs of either the Army of Republika Srpska or the population at large. Whenever the population received provisions, it brought relief to troops as they could focus on defence rather than worry about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you now call up 65 ter document 00777D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, how did the Main Staff view the donations coming from such organisations locally? We'll have a look at a document. Did the Main Staff support such self-organised efforts or was it opposed to them?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff supported all manner of aid whilst working toward having some sort of control over the aid by placing it into a central storage facility where the army would be able to manage them. The Main Staff was aware of the focal points which needed aid and where such goods needed to be siphoned to. There were disorganised ways of dealing with aid locally so that some units would have aid in stock while others would be lacking the necessary assets which would enable them to complete their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Main Staff fully informed of the assets received by units at lower levels?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can definitely be said is that there was no reliable information as to the quantities involved. At the local level due to the various quarters exerting influence, including political influence, there was a need for control, and this caused concern for the Main Staff. Primarily, as I said, because priorities needed to be identified and assets needed to be redirected where they were needed most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document that we have on our screen. We looked at it during proofing. Were you familiar with this order issued by the commander of the Main Staff on the very topic we discussed just now?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I may not have seen this specific order but there were orders of this kind and quite a few which came from the Main Staff. There was chaos, if I can put it that way. Everyone -- well, not everyone, many tried to get their hands on this sort of assistance in the form of assets and equipment in order to secure their own rating, as it were, at the local level. Rating or standing. And it led to some anomalies. There were war profiteers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have a number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D465. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we've come to the issue of donations, I have two more follow-up questions. Were you aware of the instances of individual donations coming from citizens of the Republika Srpska in relation to their duty to do their military service? What was the situation in that quarter?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with some specific cases and some that I only heard of. There was one businessman who was a native of Sokolac. He showed me a receipt testifying to his donation made for the defence effort which had been signed for him personally by President Radovan Karadzic. And based on this donation, he was thus released of his duty to do his military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the amount involved in this donation?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the amount was in excess of 300.000 German marks. I can't recall the exact amount, though. This individual, whose name I forgot, I knew because he socialised frequently, and I don't know on what basis, and was in contact with my superior, Colonel -- or rather, General Stevan Tomic. That's how I knew the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it you heard of him? You said that -- or rather, what was it that you heard of such donations? You said that you had personal knowledge and second-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion I told my best man, who was my best man at my wedding in 1994 in Bijeljina, I told him the story. He laughed upon hearing it and said that it was a ridiculous sum because in Bijeljina individuals of this sort - let's call them businessmen - would give as many as several million marks to that end. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Ivan Lesic? Milan Lesic.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of him. I believe that I even had the chance of making his acquaintance at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the issue of donations, what can you tell us about Milan Lesic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Lesic was one of those individuals who brought to the Main Staff the aid coming from an association of citizens from Canada, I believe. And not just once; I believe he did that on several occasions. I think it was mostly in 1994 and 1995 that he brought the aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to this particular association from Canada, were there other diaspora associations that provided donations to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were. People came from the far-flung Australia, Switzerland, Germany, France.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know of any such donations coming from the diaspora at lower levels, i.e., at the level of brigades and corps?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From conversations with individuals down on the ground, i.e., corps, the financial organs of the corps to which my administration was a superior organ by the speciality line, by the chain of command line, it was the corps command that was their superior, indicated that such donations were even more ample or abundant at the local level because people would make donations to their native areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what is war booty and did it exist as an extra budgetary source of income for the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means there was war booty which included real assets, I don't recall there being financial assets, and they could be used in the service of the defence effort in order to provide supplies to the army. These were, therefore, materiel assets. This is as far as I know. It was the logistics sector of the Main Staff which was charged with this area as well as the commands of the units down in the field. Such assets could include vehicles, foodstuffs, ammunition at times as well, and any other goods. The cattle stock, that's something I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to these sources of income for the Army of Republika Srpska, were there other ways and means of obtaining monies, and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In truth there were. There were some sources of revenue which were absurd, if I can put it that way. The influx of foreign currency assets came to a treasury that was set up by the Main Staff of the VRS was the result of -- or rather, there was also the revenue based on income made as a result of loaning heavy artillery to the HVO in around Sarajevo, possibly even on the Herzegovina front and perhaps even elsewhere, which were subsequently repossessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you quite specifically about what you've just told us. What it is that you give and what it is that you get in return, tell us in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made decisions to give or rent such property, if you want. This was heavy weaponry, heavy artillery pieces that were rented out, basically. In return, we would be paid a certain compensation. In foreign currency, of course. As far as I remember, the first time such foreign currency monies were received, they could have amounted to 30.000 German marks, I think, but not all such activities could, in fact, be detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what you just mentioned a moment ago, this foreign currency treasury, can you tell us where it was and what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska there was a foreign currency treasury which was set up pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. The source of income for the treasury were certainly the donations similar to the ones that you have mentioned in respect to Mr. Lesic, as well as some other donations that I mentioned, which were not as big as the former ones. Certain monies were also withdrawn from the bank. The head of the foreign currency treasury was me and I was appointed as the head of the treasury pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff. The issue and receipt of monies were carried out based exclusively on decisions issued by the commander of the the Main Staff. Such orders had to contain the following information: The monies will be used for the priority supplies of the army, primarily the procurement of fuel, and the production and procurement of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small intervention, Your Honours. Page 12, line 25. I said "donations" and the word that I read in the transcript is "nations."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually [Overlapping speakers] ... the witness has said it. I did see that. That's fine. I have a question that I would like to ask before the page disappears. You were asked, sir, at page 12 line 10: "Let me ask you quite specifically about what you have just told us. What is it that you give and what is it that you get in return? Tell us in no uncertain terms." And you say in answer: "Well, I don't know who made decisions to give or rent such property, if you want. This was heavy weaponry, heavy artillery pieces that were rented out, basically. In return, we would be paid a certain compensation, in foreign currency, of course. As far as I remember, the first time such foreign currency monies were received they could have amounted to 30.000 German marks, I think. But not all such activities could, in fact, be detected." My question is on this inability to detect. How is it so that these activities could not be detected when there were transactions between members of the VRS and other people who are renting this property? To me, this is something that actually should be obvious to everybody because there's an agreement, there's a contract here, of renting property in return for something. Can you tell us why was it difficult that some of them were not detected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I may have used an inappropriate word. I was not privy, or rather, I didn't have all the information with regard to such matters. From my point of view, I spoke about detection or things being detected. If such monies are received, if foreign currency monies are received, the record of such receipt usually stated as follows: Received from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or Received from the Herzegovina Corps, and I am talking from my own point of view, and I'm saying that I was not always privy to the sources of such receivables. And that's why I used the word "detect." Only from my point of view, I was not always able to detect where the monies came from. Those people who were in charge of such activities, who implemented such money transactions, of course they knew where the money came from, but I myself did not have all the information at my disposal. And when you asked about the weaponry that was issued alone, of course I, as an economist, as a finance man, didn't need to hear more but the words "heavy artillery," cannons, howitzers. There were other people that were more versed in heavy artillery. I was not one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session, Your Honours, just for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now, let's go back to the foreign currency treasury. You've explained the procedure for us. When an order is issued, and you did mention orders for the withdrawal of monies, so when you received such an order, what did you do? How did the procedure evolve?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we had received an order on the setting up of the treasury and on appointing its head. Later on, the commander of the Main Staff issued decisions on the use of the foreign currency amounts. We prepared those decisions in the administration pursuant to his strict orders, and the orders were very specific as to who should receive the money for what purposes, very specifically, and whoever received the foreign currency amount in question had to report to the commander of the Main Staff in person about any task which was accomplished with the help of that money. Usually such payments were considered to be solvent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your recollection, Mr. Petrovic, how much money was paid in and paid out from that foreign currency treasury during the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my entire career I've been working with numbers. I'm really trying very hard to forget them as quickly as possible. I don't want to be burdened by figures. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to understand that whenever I mention a figure 18 or 20 years after the events, those figures can only be from memory, and if you are speaking from memory, it's difficult to say but it could have been anything between 12 and 15 million German marks. Well, there were all sorts of foreign currencies. Most payments were made in German marks but there were also American, Canadian, and Australian dollars, Swiss francs, French francs, Italian lira, Austrian shilling, English pounds as well. There may have been some other currencies, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the company called Prvi Partizan, or First Partisan in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the First Partisan, or Prvi Partizan Company, in Uzice, I heard of it, of course. It's one of the special-purpose industries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever pay a visit to the company during the war; and if you did, why?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had just one occasion to go there, to pay a visit to the First Partisan Company in Uzice. As far as I can remember, it was probably in the latter part of 1994. I accompanied the chief of the technical services. The purpose of the visit was to look at production capacities and the possibilities for this company to deliver ammunition and to be paid in foreign currency. Of course, the professional body of our administration was in charge of all that. My role was to establish whether there were any possibilities to pay the company in foreign currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about the tasks of your administration, you also mentioned accounting records. What was it that you did and that you termed bookkeeping or accountancy records?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the organisational segments of my administration was the bookkeeping and accountancy department. The task of that department was to draft certain regulations, or better said, to prepare appropriate orders that would be sent to the commander of the Main Staff for his signature. All of those documents should have been drafted with a view to establishing records and bookkeeping, or rather, records of supplies. The information of that nature was very significant in terms of the functions of control and command. That was an on-going activity, and in order to fully implement that task and in order to fully establish records both in the logistics bases as well as the -- at the level of brigades, we had to circumvent all the problems that resulted from war. At the level of brigades, there was some resistance as well to establishing the exact quantity of supplies. People didn't share that information voluntarily. Everybody wanted to hide at least some of the supplies in view of all the uncertainties as to how long the war would be going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a different topic. Did there come a time when your salaries were no longer paid? And when, and why, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the early days of the inception of the VRS were gone and the problems that we discussed at the last session were overcome, there arose problems in the payment of salaries sometime in mid-1994. Basically, salaries were not paid out as of the month of September 1994. Based on what I knew about it, this was due to some political decisions. I'm referring to the salaries due to the members of the VRS, which were financed and paid out through the accountancy centre of the Ministry of Defence of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your emotive response to hearing that payments were no longer paid out? How did you react to that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was indignant about it. It wasn't a positive experience. We tried to overcome this, not to have it impact our spirits, and we went on about carrying out our tasks. Let me add that there were 20 of us in the Main Staff -- or rather, that those of us who were in the Main Staff worked around the clock, 24 hours a day. We gave it our all, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that any of the officers who received salaries from that source decided to leave the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody left the ranks of the Army of Republika Srpska for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that point when you no longer received your salary, were you paid out any sort of a compensation; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall sometime in September General Tomic arriving and saying that again in some political quarters a decision was taken to provide non-commissioned and commissioned officers of the VRS, as he put it in his very words, a one-time loan. We did indeed receive it. I think we were paid out 200 dinars, roughly, across the board, the same amount to all. He, of course, was not the one who provided the money. He delegated the obligation to the financial bodies of the corps and the financial organ of the staff. In other words, on to those bodies that were charged with executing such tasks for certain organisational units. As far as I remember, he said that, depending on who it would be who would be paying our salaries, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska or the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- or rather, regardless of who it would be who would pay out this sum, we would definitely have to pay that money back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Members of the VRS who did not receive their monies from the FRY, did they receive any sort of additional fringes to the salary, any sort of bonds?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you mean those -- you were asking about those who did not receive their salary from the FRY, but rather from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they received the salaries in the amount that they existed, however little it was. I was charged with that. However, they received other forms of aid which were higher in value than the salary itself, in terms of foodstuffs and other sort of assistance that they would receive in their local communities from companies who were able to provide such aid. As I said, such aid was much higher in value than the salaries that they received, even higher than the salary received by the VRS members who were paid them out through the accounting centre of the Ministry of Defence of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session for a brief moment again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter document of the Defence 00763D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that document, may I just find out from the witness, Mr. Petrovic, you indicated that there was a time in 1994 when the salaries of the officers who were paid from the FRY were not paid. Was there ever a time when the salaries of soldiers who were paid by the Republika Srpska were not paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards salaries financed from the budget of Republika Srpska via the Ministry of Defence intended for the VRS members, there existed problems of a different nature. Whenever assets were set aside, the problem was of actually having money in cash since the amount required for the salaries was very high. But there was not a period when salaries were not paid at all. There were periods when salaries were paid belatedly. Other remedies were sought to address the situation, for instance, where there was not enough money in cash and the amount required was perhaps even as high as 180.000, the remedy was to print securities or bonds in lieu of money. These were like coupons that could be exchanged for foodstuffs with certain companies, which soldiers could take home for their families. It was only logical that if one of the corps was paid in such coupons that -- one month, that the next month that particular corps would be paid in money and another corps would receive coupons. There were late payments but there were no instances when salaries were not paid at all. Are you happy with my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I have a question in relation to what you said on page 19, line 14 and 15. Basically, you said, salaries were not paid out as of the month of September 1994. "Based on what I knew about it, this was due to some political decisions." I would like you to elaborate on the political decisions you referred to in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interruption in the payment of salaries was between September and February, unless I'm mistaken. Unfortunately, I did not hold such a position at such a level that would enable me to be familiar with all the developments in the policies of either the civilian or military bodies. The information I had was one that could reach me as a captain 1st class. I didn't always have all the necessary information. At any rate, this was probably the result of some sort of disagreement between the leadership of the FRY and the political leadership of Republika Srpska, a disagreement surrounding the way in which the war activities were to unfold or stop, in fact. I was a lower-ranking officer, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up on the question put by His Honour Mr. David. Did you hear of the Contact Group Plan for the resolution of the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. There were several such plans. I don't know exactly what the time-line was, the Contact Group Plan, Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a time when a decision was made to impose sanctions on Republika Srpska on the part of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this. One of the elements entailed by the sanctions was the interruption of the payment of salaries, which ensued in the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document has to do with His Honour Moloto's question. This is a report of the Ministry of the Interior which deals, however, with the payment of salaries of the members of the 1st and 2nd Romanija units, and can you first tell us, the units mentioned in this document, who did they receive their salaries from?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 1st and 2nd Romanija Brigades which belonged to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps received their salaries from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is self-explanatory. What I'm interested in -- or, rather, have a look at the document and then I'll have a question.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's the problem I discussed earlier on, namely, when at some point there would not be sufficient cash and they would resort to coupons, which were not a very popular choice. They could be used only in some companies which had appropriate goods, such as foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm interested in. In the last paragraph, we see a comment made by the signatory of the document. Since you were familiar with the issue of salaries, did you know that such difficulties in the payment of salaries had a bearing on the regular military activities and proper fulfillment of tasks? Did anyone refuse to carry out their tasks on this account?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, there were no such reactions in response to the non-payment of salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so assigned. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D466.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the last session we spoke of the foreign currency treasury kept by the Main Staff and you spoke of the assets that were earmarked there. Can you tell us, sir, when exactly the treasury was set up. I think your previous answer was an approximation.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was just before the end of 1992, and it all started with the case I related here, namely, the renting of heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this period between the end of 1992 through to the end of the war in 1995, was there a period when the influx of monies into that treasury was higher? Was it in the early days or at a later date?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the early days the influx of assets was rather modest. What I can say, in retrospect, that as the popularity of the commander of the Main Staff grew, so did the influx of monies into that treasury increase, so 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now the last topic, Mr. Petrovic, and that is your transfer into the Army of Yugoslavia. At the beginning of your testimony we heard that you joined the Army of Yugoslavia in 1999 sometime, in the spring of that year. Let me ask you, before that had you expressed a desire, had you applied to be transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia; and if so, when, approximately, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in 1996, after the end of the war, I applied to become a member of the Army of Yugoslavia. I had been irritated and dissatisfied as a result of all the problems that could be felt after 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Problems where?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, not because the commander of the Main Staff had been removed at a certain point but because I had experienced different problems in addition to the two and a half months long complete blockade of my unit in Zagreb, followed by the blockade in Bihac, I had experienced a third blockade which affected me the most. Due to some internal conflicts within the leadership of the Army of Republika Srpska, the removal of the commander of the Main Staff, a lot of MUP members, perhaps even battalions, surrounded the Main Staff building and held it under siege, as it were, for a few days. I didn't find it easy to cope with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the permission of the Court, I would like to add another document to our 65 ter list. It's a document from Mr. Petrovic's personnel file. I marked it as 04010D. Could Ms. Carter please say -- state her opinion, and then I would like to show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I could get some clarification for the documents. Unfortunately, I was never given the 65 ter numbers, I only have e-mail document 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a request -- just a second, I can give you the ERN number. 0677-5448 for the B/C/S version. It is a letter written by several officers who applied to be transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to the use of this document. I would seek for it to be MFI'd until we can get a read-through for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may use the document, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I meant, yes. What we can see here is a document dated 13 December, although in the English version I can see that the date is July. Mr. Zorko must have made a mistake when he translated this. But let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the date?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, it's not easy to see the date. It is the 13th. Is it December? I don't know, it's typed in letters. It should be December 199 ... It should read December, the 13th December, right? The 13th December, 1996. Those are the dates towards the end of the year when, according to an unwritten rule, transfer applications were filed. It was usually done towards the end of the year, hence the 13th December, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, under 2, who is that? Whose information is this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrovic, Rajko, son of Marinko, captain 1st class. That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Just awhile ago you gave us your motives and reasons for leaving in 1996, or rather, for applying to be transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia. What happened after your application was filed? What was the decision made and on whose behalf?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The application that I filed -- I don't know about the others -- was turned down a priori, and I believe that that came from the Main Staff, and I don't know whether the name in the 1996 was still the Main Staff or perhaps the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, I was not allowed to join the Army of Yugoslavia. The Main Staff turned me down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that time in 1996 did you know, were you aware of any needs of the Army of Yugoslavia to apply experts of your type?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, experts of my profile were always in short supply. This is corroborated by the fact that the administration that I worked for only employed three people although by establishment there should have been 10 employees. And I believe that the situation was similar, if not the same, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm sure that there was room for me per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be MFI'd, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D467, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings my examination-in-chief to an end. Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic, for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for your understanding and I would also like to thank the Presiding Judge and the other members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have just a brief moment to consult with co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we could please move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in your --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hold, please. We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, this morning you were discussing Milan Lesic. Can you tell me if -- what monies did Milan Lesic give to the VRS after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, after the Dayton Accords, I don't remember that he donated anything. I remember that he arrived sometime in 1994 and 1995. I don't know if anything happened after the Dayton Accords. The Dayton Accords were signed towards the very end of the war, so I don't know if there was any influx of money. I can't tell you the exact dates, but I know that he turned up on a couple of occasions, that he attended meetings with General Mladic and General Tomic. I also attended a meeting on one occasion, and as far as I can remember, on that occasion I read a letter sent in by an association of citizens from Vancouver that described efforts and support that they extended to us in that way as well. And he recorded that, as far as I can remember, if that's the occasion in question. He actually videoed the entire event. And I suppose that that was Milan Lesic, that he was the one who was there when I was reading that letter. It was a long time ago, mind you, and after the Dayton Accords, I really can't identify the time and say whether he turned up after that, whether he brought any money after that, and if he did, what currency it was in. I said that the foreign currency treasury was made up of some ten different foreign currencies. I don't know what Milan Lesic brought in, whether it was Canadian dollars or American dollars, I really don't know. You are asking me things that my brain does not even want to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, so that we can finish quickly, when you have told us once that you don't know, you don't have to repeat yourself many times. Just cut your sentence -- your answers short. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll stop explaining, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I asked you about the VRS payments. Do you know about the payments that Milan Lesic made to General Mladic after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought he said he doesn't know about any payments by Milan Lesic after the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had asked initially in relation to the VRS. Now I'm asking particularly as a separate issue in relation to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you discussed earlier today about the cessation of your salary payments in September of 1994. I'd like to explore your salary a bit. Can you tell us, up to this point, how much were you being paid monthly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 the practice reverted to the convertible dinar. Rather, the convertible dinar was introduced. Because there was not enough funds and because it was impossible to secure the requisite amount of the convertible dinar, salaries were paid out in various installments. At some points, the salaries amounted to 20 dinars, in others to 40 convertible dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please listen to the question and try to be as brief as you possibly can. The question is very simple and straightforward: What was your monthly salary up until September 1994? A million dinar, 10.000 dinar, two dinar; that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It varied from month to month. 100, 150, 200, 250, up to 450, 500. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's sort of agree on one point, Mr. Petrovic. We understand that, because of the shortage of cash, it fluctuated. However, what were you entitled to as a salary up until that time, whether you did get it or not. I guess this is the question, ma'am. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No two months was the salary the same. It always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you there. In terms of the paper on contract when you were told now you are now 1st class captain, and this is now 1994 September, what were you supposed to be paid, if the money was there? You can tell us what -- My salary was supposed to be 100 dinar per month, however, because of the the problems no two months did I get a consistent figure. One day I got one dinar, the next day I got 1.000 dinar. But what was the legal entitlement in terms of your salary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps before the month of September it amounted to 600 dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated after September of 1994 that you had become indignant due to the cessation of those payments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was indignance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were others who were similar to your situation also indignant?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were individual cases, I suppose, and I wasn't there to assess the level of the morale; some were more indignant, others less.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, there was a change in morale after the cessation; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, and I'm judging by how I felt, I tried to gather strength to continue performing my duties. What I was able to observe did not indicate that there were any disruptions in the activities of the VRS, and particularly not in those of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated at some point a loan was given. Can you tell us when that loan was received?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the second half of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you recall the general --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you recall the general amount of that loan?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received 200 dinars, as did everybody else across the board, non-commissioned and commissioned officers alike. As far as I remember, the amount involved was of some 500.000 dinars, which corresponded to the head count of non-commissioned and commissioned officers of the VRS. If you multiply the number of officers with 200 dinars, it amounted to 500 dinars, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Moving on from September 1994, you ultimately made a claim within the military courts for payment of those five months of salary, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat again the date that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm saying moving on from September 1994, subsequent to that time did you make a claim within the military courts to receive payment for those five months?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't approach the military court right away. I filed my claim with the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I think that prior to that I wrote to the 30th Personnel Centre. Now, the Main Staff, or rather, the individual charged with these duties, General Skrbic, did, as far as I remember, issue a decision whereby I was entitled to the amount of pay due to me. This was a result of an internal agreement between me and Mr. Skrbic. We agreed that this was to be a sort of guinea pig, or a trial, because our status in law remained the same whereas our salaries were not forthcoming, so this constituted a sort of challenge to me at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The status under law, according to that decision, is that you as a professional soldier of the Yugoslav Army had to have your salary calculated on the basis of those regulations; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The status, which remained as it was through the 30th Personnel Centre and which constituted a way of payment of salaries and providing assistance to the families of members of the VRS was in fact the basis through which we exercised our entitlements --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- through the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you were transferred to the Military Post 3001, which corresponds to the 30th Personnel Centre, on the order of the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Perisic, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself didn't know, nor was it within my power to know this, who took the decision to set up the 30th Personnel Centre as an administration and overseeing vehicle which kept track of those former JNA personnel who became members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a way, in my view, of --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you've answered my question. I'd then like to move on to --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Before we leave the topic of your salary, I'd like to call up P2817.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what you have before you is a letter from General Mladic in which he is expressing concern about these salaries. He has indicated that as of the date November 4th of 1994, that: "This situation has been created in which attention is unnecessarily drawn from combat tasks and people are now focused on solving this problem and deferring of this issue is making the matters worse for professional soldiers of the VJ and their families." Sir, were you aware of these occurrences in November 4th of 1994?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document does not originate from my administration. It came from the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs, so General Skrbic, who was the head the administration, could have been familiar with this document. It must have been drafted under his authority. I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware at this time that meetings were being held with the VJ in order to solve the problem in a way that is acceptable to all, and in fact in the last few days they had requested from the VJ General Staff to solve the salary issue as soon as possible as it was the case with other VJ members? Were you aware of those occurrences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the witness, the document should be turned to page 2 in the B/C/S so that what Madam Carter has read out the witness can read for himself. We don't have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With all due respect, the -- what I was reading from, actually, if the numbers do line up, should actually be on the first page. They were numbered number 2 and 3 of the first series.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Ms. Carter read out just now was on page 2 in the B/C/S, under items 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Since I cannot read B/C/S, I'll defer to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Since I cannot read B/C/S, I'll defer to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 2, I'll read this out and Ms. Carter will say if this is really the portion she intended to read out. Mr. Petrovic, please read item 1 aloud and slowly and we'll see if it has to do with Ms. Carter's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2: "The problems arisen around the abolishment of salaries should be resolved across the board as well as for all the members of the VJ, in keeping with the systematic practices, merits, and gravity of the tasks carried out by us. In this way, we will do our best to preserve the dignity of our task and profession."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What Ms. Carter read out is under item 3 on page 1, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you now deferring to Madam Carter insofar as knowledge of the B/C/S is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I think that's scary for all involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, for your ease, I'm pointing out there's several enumerated small passages in the middle of the page. The pieces that I was recently reading were actually number 2 and number 3. Ultimately were you aware of the meetings that the VRS was holding with the VJ in order to solve the salary problems?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the collegium of the Main Staff, or rather, a member of the collegium of General Mladic. Based on some information that I got on the record and off the record, I heard discussions were taking place with the government of the VRS to have payments made through that channel and other discussions as well. I didn't have any specific information. Perhaps Mr. Tomic, who was the head of the administration, did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, it would be helpful if you say No, I didn't have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Moving on from number 3, it indicates: "These measures that we have taken have not given any concrete results yet, but we are not going to stop finding solutions to this problem." Sir, this implies that no loan had taken place by November 4th of 1994.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why this should imply it since I received 200 dinars. It was a one-off payment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, going back to your service, you had indicated that by April of 1999 you had transferred into a division of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into a brigade of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I have indication from your personnel file that that took place, that the re-assignment took place on 15 April 1999, does that correspond or jog your memory as to the day you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been the 18th [as interpreted] of April under any circumstances. I know that for a fact. My transfer took place shortly after the commencement of bombing. The order dated back to that period whereas I was able to transfer between the 5th and the 10th of April. The 18th of April is too late a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Choosing the transfer date between the 5th and 10th of April, you referred to some bombing. At that point in time are you referring to the declaration of war that had been declared in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 23rd of March and what transpired in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of March, 1994, a declaration of imminent threat of war was established in the former Yugoslavia, with the declaration taking place on the 24th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the year that I heard is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I believe I said 1999, but I do see 1994 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My distinct apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, on 23rd March of 1999 an imminent threat of war was declared, following the next day with a declaration of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only a state of an imminent threat of war was declared. As far as I know, a state of war was never declared. I'm telling you what I know, but there are more pertinent individuals who can talk about it, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I do have just a few more minutes with the general, however, I do see that it's a break. I'll be finished in less than five minutes. I'll leave it to the Court as to what they'd like to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the warring parties at issue were the Kosovo Liberation Army, NATO, and the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia and pursuant to a decision taken by the government of the FRY, I am only mandated to answer the questions concerning the financing of the VRS, my status within the VRS, some questions about the 30th Personnel Centre. I do not have authorisation from the government to talk about any other issues. I don't have the mandate of the government of the Republika Srpska to answer any other questions, so please bear that in mind. And even if I was authorised to discuss these matters, I am not the best person to talk about them. I don't have the requisite knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, I see you are standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clarify: We know that this is an active officer of the Army of Serbia and he was released from his duty to keep the state secret, and this is precisely what he was discussing, the waiver that was given for the ICTY in respect to certain issues, and that's the government of the Republic of Serbia, let me add that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, it looks like this is getting protracted. We might as well take our break now and come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll try to ask my line of questioning in a way that doesn't offend the waiver that you possess. Can you tell me, was the VRS a part of the hostilities that began on March 23rd of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the Army of Republika Srpska a part of the hostilities? Which army? The Army of Republika Srpska? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When we left off before, I was trying to confirm who was involved in the bombing that you were referring to at the end of March. I had initially asked you if the warring parties were NATO, the VJ, and the KLA, and you took issue with that question. So I'm trying to ask you in reverse, was the VRS a part of that bombardment campaign?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia immediately after the beginning of bombing. I mentioned the beginning of that bombing campaign only because about that time I was transferred and became a member of the Army of Yugoslavia. I'm not a strategic leader so I have no way of knowing what was done at the strategic level and who did it, but I don't think it was involved, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you you personally were not involved in any activities in March of 1999 in relation to the bombardment campaign?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, throughout my entire career I have dealt with finances in different militaries, the JNA, the Army of Republika Srpska, and to this very day I only deal with financial issues. This is my area of expertise. And when you are putting these questions to me, it is almost the same as if you were to ask me how to do an open heart surgery. You should ask a heart surgeon how do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, if this question is not covered by your waiver, then the question is very simple. You are a financial person, you have right through your professional life practiced your financial expertise within armies. The question is, were you yourself involved, did take any part, in whatever capacity, during the hostilities that took place in March 1999 in Kosovo and the FRY? Now, start off by telling us whether your waiver bars you from answering the question, and if it doesn't, carry on to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My task to testify here is relative to the Army of Republika Srpska and those duties that I discharged in the Main Staff with regard to finance. I've never been involved in any acts or misdeeds or anything else but that mission of mine which is finances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are still not answering the question, sir. You can tell us if you feel you don't want to answer the question for whatever reason, but if you feel you have to answer the question, then you must answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not involved in any activities of a military nature, military movements, or any such activities. I dealt with finances. I was in Belgrade at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, did you deal with any financial issues within any army during the bombing on the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a mandate and I can only talk about financing and the issue of financing of the Army of Republika Srpska. My mandate does not extend any further. I am now employed by the Army of Serbia. I'm involved in finances, in financial issues, and I don't think that this Tribunal is concerned with what I do today. Please spare me from answering questions that I'm not capable of answering. There have been so many other people who have testified before this Honourable Chamber, other generals. It is not that I don't want to answer. I either can't answer because I do not know or I do not have the mandate to answer them. But primarily I don't know, I can't answer your question because I don't know, I don't know anything about any strategic issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was very simple and you should know because it involves your personal involvement. The question was simply whether you yourself, in any capacity within any army, you were involved in the hostilities that took place in March 1999. Now, you can say you don't have the right to answer that question but you can't say you don't know. You would know if did you something or didn't do something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, I didn't hear, you started off with "I was not in --" and then the interpretation wasn't complete. Madam Interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was complete. The witness didn't continue because the B/C/S interpretation was going on at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir, are you able to answer, then? What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not involved in any hostilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you arrived in Belgrade between the 5th and the 10th of April, 1999. I would like to know, which army were you serving in between March 23rd, 1999, and the date you arrived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would seek to use a portion of this gentleman's personnel file that's been uploaded as XN418, and as that is new evidence, we seek leave from the Court to be able to present that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Ms. Carter tell us the purpose for which she wishes to use these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For impeachment only, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to call up XN418. The B/C/S page will be 89. And the English translation that I'm interested in is 0677-6350.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the document that you have before you makes up a portion of your personnel file and it addresses the years of pensionable service of your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated between March 23rd, 1999, until the time that you arrived in Belgrade between the 5th and the 10th of April, you were a member of the VRS. However, you received additional pension consideration for being a part of war service in the VJ beginning 24 March 1999. Can you tell me how you as a VRS officer received war-time credit beginning at the Kosovo bombardment?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this be zoomed in a little, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether this is serving the purposes that you want to achieve. If you see that even the dates before that date you are referring to he is always referred to as a VJ officer and he has always said that even when he was in the VRS he was paid from the FRY, and we have heard ample evidence here to that effect, that for purposes of payment and benefits and pension, he was regarded as VJ soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The distinction here, however, is that those same soldiers, when they were receiving war-time credit, they always received it in relation to a war in which the VRS were participating. In the case of this witness, however, he was receiving war-time credit for what was occurring completely within the confines of the FRY and, more specifically, in relation to the Kosovo conflict. That's what makes this witness different than the other ones that we've heard because there's been a separation between Kosovo and the service that we've seen there and these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I don't understand you, but carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you were a VRS officer at the inception of the Kosovo conflict. Can you tell me why you were receiving war time double counting of your pension?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say why the date is 24th of March, 1999. At that time I was in the Main Staff in Bijeljina, so I really can't say, I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness and I pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Mr. Lukic, any re-examination? Mr. Lukic, before you start, what do you want to do with this exhibit, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it be admitted into evidence and please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2929. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Madam Carter asked you on page 42, line 7 of today's LiveNote if you are aware that you you became a member of the 30th Personnel Centre pursuant to General Perisic's order. And you answered. My question is this: You've told us about your status entitlements in the year 1992 when you became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, that was during the war. Before this Trial Chamber we've heard testimonies about the 30th Personnel Centre to have been established on the 30th of November. My question to you, sir, is this: Did your status rights change in any way from 1992 to 1995, or were they absolutely the same all the time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the same all that time save for one period when payments were interrupted for four months during the year 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry. I am sorry. I am sorry. Mr. Petrovic, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony here. Thank you very much for taking the time to come and testify. You are now excused, you may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, I would like to thank you for having given me an opportunity to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth, as the declaration goes, and I hope that what I've testified about will contribute at least a little to the outcome of this case and the acquittal of this honourable man and exquisite professional, General Perisic. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. You are now excused and may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is ready to appear in this courtroom on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then, in that event, we will stand adjourned to Monday, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.49 p.m.
